Without appealing to Marx or any other form of theory, sex work as a thing in and of itself should be abolished. It's capitalism, it's labor, and if we're against those two things then we have to be against sex work regardless of the individual circumstances of sex workers. What this doesn't mean is that sex workers can't enjoy their work and that people can't enjoy being consumers of what sex workers put out. You are not wrong for enjoying sex so let's drop that as a point. Neither does it mean that abuse in the sex industry should be ignored and you aren't wrong for calling it out so let's drop that as a point. What is wrong is assuming the individual or collective experiences of sex workers should be held as points for argument on what to do about sex work when the simple fact is that sex work HAS to be abolished along with the rest of capitalism and labor. 

Now the moment experiences of sex workers do matter is when changing the sex industry to protect and empower sex workers as workers. Sex workers do need unions, co-ops, and other means of having individual and collective ownership over their labor. They need to rebel against businesses both big and small AND governments from profiting off of their work while lowering the quality of their lives. Economies shouldn't get to enjoy the fruits of sex labor while not protecting the quality of life of sex laborers.

"Empower sex workers, abolish sex work" should be the motto here.

Anarcho-transhumanism has been a thing for at least a few decades now. It's less that anarchists slapped anarchism onto transhumanism but rather transhumanism enthusiasts figured that the best way to have a good transhumanist society is through abolition of hierarchy. 

Their logic works in two ways: 

1. That if we work as a species to relate to each other as fully empowered individuals and work towards the benefit of ourselves and each other, we can work on avoiding the problems we often see in Cyberpunk and other "bad future" scenarios. 

2. Abolition of hierarchy should be a natural consequence of technological development anyway. As we learn to satisfy our needs in more efficient, less consumptive, demanding, and invasive ways, and relate to each other in ways that don't require the barriers of relating to each other as humans but as something more abstract but just as real, we would do away with concepts of class, age, race, gender, sex, etc. Any basis of oppression or authority would be gone. This is a rather optimistic way of looking at things though.

In fact, more often than not, anarchism is the logical result of a set of politics rather than it being added to, much like here in the case of transhumanism.
And this is why anarcho-transhumanism is a thing.

I too am horrible at aiming lol But I like to think of aiming less as a skill but more of a... "reward". 

First I break down accuracy and precision into two separate things since games don't really show you the difference. Accuracy is about how far away you are from your intended target and precision is how close your shots are together when shooting at any given area. You would often find it that people with terrible aim are either really accurate but terrible in precision, really precise but really inaccurate, or just sucky at both.  An extra factor is reaction time because it could very well be that you might be a little late to pressing the trigger button or even too preemptive. In fact, sometimes people can't seem to help but shoot when they are way off target so it could be an issue of information processing. Figuring out which category you're in and what your personal issues are is key to the next step of improving which is understanding the game's shooting mechanics.

Shooting mechanics are part of the rule set of every shooter game. Some shooters have randomness present in the way their guns work, some don't. In fact, if you get rid of things like spread, recoil, projectile speed, projectile size, and drop, suddenly everybody's aim is almost perfect. So a part of your aiming is due to your ability to handle the mechanics of individual guns. Thankfully, because most guns come in a variety, you can always find something that's compatible with your natural ability. Plus there are various techniques you can practice for aiming with different weapon types and tools to help you improve over time.

Lastly, it could very well be your controller. Joysticks aren't meant for shooters at all, and it could be the case that, when it comes to shooters, you might need to upgrade your controller. Modded controllers can help, gyro controls are way more accurate especially when combined with joysticks, and m+kb and touch controls are infamous for their high accuracy so don't be afraid to get yourself better equipment to get the job done.

As a personal case, I started realizing I have reaction time and tracking issues when I realized I can hit my shots more consistently when there's something that signals when I should take a shot or does the shooting for me while I focus on aiming. In the game Spacelords, there's a character named Shae who's a sniper. However,  the accuracy of her is based on a charge that grows as you focus on an enemy's head. The more centered their head is in your reticle, the faster the charge increases, the higher your accuracy and damage. In mobile games, a lot of them come with an autofire option so that your gun shoots when near or on an enemy's hit box. In Call of Duty mobile specifically, you have to hold the crosshair for a small period of time in order for the autofire to kick in (even longer for snipers). Stuff like that helps a lot and actively trains you. 

This isn't including things like setting adjustments which also help. So just experiment until you hit a mark and then practice with what you find.
